why_wrong: Length raises the cost of brute force, but a long password built from common words or predictable patterns is still broken quickly by a dictionary attack; strength comes from unpredictability, not length alone
real_world_consequence: A user picks a long but guessable passphrase, believes they are safe, and the account is taken over

statement: Changing passwords often makes accounts safer
why_wrong: Forced periodic rotation pushes people toward predictable increments (Summer2026!, Fall2026!) and does nothing if the credential is already leaked; NIST SP 800-63B recommends against it
real_world_consequence: Weaker, more predictable passwords plus a false sense of security

statement: Multi-factor authentication makes an account impossible to hack
why_wrong: MFA raises the cost of attack substantially but is bypassable via SIM swap, MFA-fatigue push spam, session-token theft, and real-time phishing proxies
real_world_consequence: The user stops maintaining a strong password, removing a whole layer of defense
